mappings.note: asks for a60 and then for the sum of the last 10 terms as separate parts; the second needs a51 as well, so both formulas are marked in their own right
same two-part shape -- last term by a+(n-1)d, then a partial sum over indices 36 to 50; two stated asks, two outcomes
Sn given as a quadratic; both the AP and the nth term are obtained by differencing successive sums, so the sum is the object under test
the sum-and-product condition on a3 and a7 is setup (and yields two cases); the single ask is S20, so coded on the sum demand
5-mark duplicate of the Sm = Sn proof; factorising the sum formula is the whole argument
the series total is given and the LAST TERM is wanted, so the count k is first found from Sn and then converted; the entry point is the sum formula
part one counts the terms of a printed AP from its last term (nth-term formula, not a described set), part two sums a shifted AP; two separate demands
an identity among sums of n, 2n and 3n terms, proved symbolically; no term is ever evaluated
the 'sum of three middle terms' collapses to 3x by symmetry, so no Sn formula is used; the work is locating index 19 and stepping to the last three terms -- LO-2
5-mark duplicate of the four-consecutive-terms ratio item; the a-3d..a+3d device rests only on the constant difference

digits modelled as a-d, a, a+d (LO-1's constant step) and then translated into place value; the contextual translation earns C-3.2-LO-1, though most of the marks are place-value algebra rather than AP work
a real participation context with a months-to-years unit conversion; the total ages force a quadratic in n through Sn, and only then does a+(n-1)d give the eldest age
chase problem: the pursuer's distances form an AP that must be summed and equated to the thief's uniform distance; modelling plus the sum formula, no indexed term asked
the AP is built from a remainder description and counted (225 terms), the middle index is evaluated, and the two flanking blocks are summed -- all three demands are separately stated
same three demands on a remainder-1-mod-3 set between 9 and 95; honestly the identical outcome set to the mod-4 item, so no distinction is invented
prize money is exactly the 'savings/instalments' context LO-1 names; the total is given and the first prize is recovered from Sn, with no index asked

asks how many rows (a count of terms from the situation, LO-2) and then the total number of plants (LO-1's contextual solve via Sn); both asks are stated, unlike the prize items which ask only a value
seven cash prizes with a fixed decrement and a known total; n is given, so nothing is counted -- modelling plus the sum formula only
a loan repayment in rising instalments where the only ask is HOW LONG, i.e. the number of terms, reached through a quadratic from Sn; the count is the demand, so LO-2 of C-3.2 rather than LO-1
a geometric context where the semicircle lengths must first be seen to be pi times an AP of radii; the ask is a single total, so the sum formula finishes it
a ratio of sums converted into a ratio of indexed terms; like the (7n+1):(4n+27) item, the content IS the link between the two formulas, so both are cited
house numbers modelled as 1..49 with sums on either side of an unknown position; the existence proof runs entirely on the sum of the first n naturals
salary case study comparing two firms: parts (i)-(ii) are 15-year totals and parts (iii)-(iv) are tenth-year salaries, so the sum and the nth term are each marked twice
investment context: the yearly increase is d recovered from a1 and a11 via the nth-term formula, and the accrued income is a separate sum demand
decaying swing arcs modelled with negative d; part (i) asks the tenth arc and part (ii) the distance travelled, so both formulas are separately required
